items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Demand for which PED equals 1, so the percentage change in quantity demanded equals the percentage change in price"?
options: price inelastic demand
unit elastic demand
necessity (income inelastic normal good)
Engel's law
items.answer: unit elastic demand
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of unit elastic demand.

items.stem: Explain why PED is measured using percentage changes rather than absolute changes.
items.answer: Percentages make the measure independent of units (litres, kilograms, dollars, euros), so elasticities can be compared across goods and countries.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Percentages make the measure independent of units (litres, kilograms, dollars, euros), so elasticities can be compared across goods and countries. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between perfectly inelastic demand and perfectly elastic demand.
items.answer: Perfectly elastic demand (PED = ∞) is horizontal: any price rise reduces quantity to zero; perfectly inelastic demand (PED = 0) is vertical: quantity does not change with price.
items.markingKey: Perfectly elastic demand (PED = ∞) is horizontal: any price rise reduces quantity to zero; perfectly inelastic demand (PED = 0) is vertical: quantity does not change with price. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The PED for train tickets in Bogotá is estimated at −0.5. Following a fare increase, the price rises by 20%. Current sales are 20,000 journeys per day. Calculate the new quantity demanded.
items.answer: 18000 journeys per day

items.stem: Elena writes: "A PED of −3 means demand is inelastic because the number is negative." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The sign only shows the inverse relationship; |PED| = 3 > 1, so demand is price elastic.
items.markingKey: The sign only shows the inverse relationship; |PED| = 3 > 1, so demand is price elastic. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain, with the help of a fully labelled diagram, the difference between price elastic and price inelastic demand.
items.answer: Two diagrams with the same price rise from P1 to P2. Elastic demand (relatively flat curve): quantity falls by a larger percentage, from Q1 to Q2, |PED| > 1. Inelastic demand (relatively steep curve): quantity falls by a smaller percentage, |PED| < 1. Label axes P and Q, and the changes in each.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Two diagrams with the same price rise from P1 to P2. Elastic demand (relatively flat curve): quantity falls by a larger percentage, from Q1 to Q2, |PED| > 1. Inelastic demand (relatively steep curve): quantity falls by a smaller percentage, |PED| < 1. Label axes P and Q, and the changes in each. IB Paper 1(a) markbands [10]: Level 4 (9-10) terms defined; clear, focused explanation; relevant, accurate and fully labelled diagram(s) that are explained. Level 3 (6-8) mostly accurate with some development. Level 2 (3-5) limited explanation or diagram errors. Level 1 (1-2) little understanding.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

When a ride-hailing company in Nairobi raised average fares from KSh 400 to KSh 460 in 2023, the number of weekly trips fell from 2.0 million to 1.7 million.
— Hypothetical company data

Calculate the PED for rides and explain what it suggests about the availability of substitutes.
items.answer: %ΔP = 15%, %ΔQ = −15%; PED = −1 (unit elastic). Consumers are fairly responsive, suggesting substitutes such as matatus and boda-bodas are available.
items.markingKey: %ΔP = 15%, %ΔQ = −15%; PED = −1 (unit elastic). Consumers are fairly responsive, suggesting substitutes such as matatus and boda-bodas are available. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Explain the range of values PED can take, using diagrams to illustrate perfectly elastic, perfectly inelastic and unit elastic demand.
items.answer: 0 (vertical), between 0 and 1 (inelastic), 1 (unit elastic – rectangular hyperbola, TR constant), >1 (elastic), ∞ (horizontal). Each with P/Q axes and interpretation.
items.markingKey: 0 (vertical), between 0 and 1 (inelastic), 1 (unit elastic – rectangular hyperbola, TR constant), >1 (elastic), ∞ (horizontal). Each with P/Q axes and interpretation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "perfectly elastic demand"?
options: How easily consumers can switch to an alternative product; the closer the substitutes, the more price elastic demand
The total amount received by firms from selling their output, equal to price × quantity sold
The price at which PED = −1 and total revenue is at its maximum
Demand for which PED is infinite: any rise in price above a given level causes quantity demanded to fall to zero, shown by a horizontal demand curve
items.answer: Demand for which PED is infinite: any rise in price above a given level causes quantity demanded to fall to zero, shown by a horizontal demand curve
items.markingKey: D. "perfectly elastic demand" is demand for which PED is infinite: any rise in price above a given level causes quantity demanded to fall to zero, shown by a horizontal demand curve.

items.stem: Briefly explain why PED values for the same good can differ between consumers.
items.answer: Responsiveness depends on income, tastes and access to substitutes; a commuter with no alternative transport has inelastic demand for train tickets while a leisure traveller who can drive has more elastic demand.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Responsiveness depends on income, tastes and access to substitutes; a commuter with no alternative transport has inelastic demand for train tickets while a leisure traveller who can drive has more elastic demand. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A cinema in Lima cuts ticket prices by 20% and ticket sales rise by 8%. Calculate PED and state whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
items.answer: PED = 8%/−20% = −0.4: price inelastic.
items.markingKey: PED = 8%/−20% = −0.4: price inelastic.

items.stem: An online retailer in Melbourne found that when it set the price of avocados at $8, it sold 400 units a month, and at $9.6 it sold 304 units. Calculate the PED, state whether demand is price elastic or inelastic, and calculate the change in total revenue. Explain whether the result is consistent with the PED value.
items.answer: PED = −1.2 (price elastic); TR changes from $3200 to $2918.4 (change of −$281.6)
items.markingKey: PED = −24%/20% = −1.2 [1]; price elastic [1]; TR: 8×400 = 3200 → 9.6×304 = 2918.4 [1]; consistent: elastic – price and TR move in opposite directions [1].

items.stem: "Price elasticity of demand values are of little practical use because they change over time." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: PED values must be updated, but they remain essential for pricing and tax policy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: PED changes with time, income and tastes; estimates are uncertain. Arguments against: estimates guide tax and pricing decisions; elasticities for many goods are fairly stable; can be re-estimated with new data. Supported judgement: PED values must be updated, but they remain essential for pricing and tax policy. Markbands (15 marks): IB Paper 1(b)/2(d) markbands [15]: Level 5 (13-15) relevant terms defined; theory explained clearly with an accurate, fully explained diagram where relevant; appropriate real-world examples; effective synthesis and a supported evaluation (short- vs long-run, stakeholders, assumptions, priorities). Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "PED along a linear demand curve".
items.answer: Elasticity falls continuously along a straight-line demand curve: elastic above the midpoint, unit elastic at the midpoint and inelastic below it
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: elasticity falls continuously along a straight-line demand curve: elastic above the midpoint, unit elastic at the midpoint and inelastic below it. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a luxury and a necessity.
items.answer: Necessities have few acceptable substitutes and inelastic demand (and income-inelastic demand); luxuries can be postponed or replaced, so their demand is more price and income elastic.
items.markingKey: Necessities have few acceptable substitutes and inelastic demand (and income-inelastic demand); luxuries can be postponed or replaced, so their demand is more price and income elastic. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why PED varies along a straight-line demand curve even though the slope is constant.
items.answer: PED = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q); ΔQ/ΔP is constant but P/Q falls as we move down the curve, so demand is elastic at high prices and low quantities and inelastic at low prices and high quantities. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: PED = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q); ΔQ/ΔP is constant but P/Q falls as we move down the curve, so demand is elastic at high prices and low quantities and inelastic at low prices and high quantities. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The demand for avocados in Singapore is Qd = 600 − 10P. Calculate the PED at a price of $8 and state whether demand is elastic or inelastic at this price.
items.answer: PED = −0.15 (price inelastic)

items.stem: Explain whether demand for Apple iPhones is likely to be more or less price elastic than demand for smartphones in general.
items.answer: More elastic: if the iPhone's price rises, consumers can switch to other brands (Samsung, Xiaomi), whereas there are few substitutes for smartphones as a whole.
items.markingKey: More elastic: if the iPhone's price rises, consumers can switch to other brands (Samsung, Xiaomi), whereas there are few substitutes for smartphones as a whole.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Brand loyalty is the most effective way for a firm to reduce the price elasticity of demand for its product.
items.answer: Brand loyalty can reduce PED significantly, but it is costly to build and may erode; product differentiation and innovation also matter.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: loyal customers do not switch to substitutes; allows higher prices without large falls in sales. Arguments against: building loyalty requires large advertising spending; competitors can innovate and win customers; low share of income or addictiveness also reduce PED. Supported judgement: Brand loyalty can reduce PED significantly, but it is costly to build and may erode; product differentiation and innovation also matter.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "PED along a linear demand curve"?
options: Demand for which PED is infinite: any rise in price above a given level causes quantity demanded to fall to zero, shown by a horizontal demand curve
Elasticity falls continuously along a straight-line demand curve: elastic above the midpoint, unit elastic at the midpoint and inelastic below it
The factors influencing price elasticity of demand: number and closeness of substitutes, necessity or luxury, proportion of income spent on the good, time period and addictiveness/habit
The distribution of the burden of an indirect tax between consumers and producers, which depends on PED and PES
items.answer: Elasticity falls continuously along a straight-line demand curve: elastic above the midpoint, unit elastic at the midpoint and inelastic below it
items.markingKey: B. "PED along a linear demand curve" is elasticity falls continuously along a straight-line demand curve: elastic above the midpoint, unit elastic at the midpoint and inelastic below it.

items.stem: "A straight-line demand curve has the same PED at every point." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: PED varies along a linear demand curve because P/Q changes: it is elastic at high prices, unit elastic at the midpoint and inelastic at low prices.
items.markingKey: PED varies along a linear demand curve because P/Q changes: it is elastic at high prices, unit elastic at the midpoint and inelastic at low prices. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A train company in Japan finds that demand for peak-time Shinkansen tickets is less price elastic than for off-peak tickets. Explain why.
items.answer: Peak travellers are often business commuters who must travel at fixed times and whose employers pay; off-peak leisure travellers can change time or mode, so they are more responsive.
items.markingKey: Peak travellers are often business commuters who must travel at fixed times and whose employers pay; off-peak leisure travellers can change time or mode, so they are more responsive.

items.stem: A demand curve is given by Qd = 100 − 2P. Explain, using calculations at P = $10, $25 and $40, how PED changes along the curve.
items.answer: PED = −2 × P/Q: at P = 10, Q = 80, PED = −0.25 (inelastic); at P = 25, Q = 50, PED = −1 (unit elastic, midpoint); at P = 40, Q = 20, PED = −4 (elastic).
items.markingKey: PED = −2 × P/Q: at P = 10, Q = 80, PED = −0.25 (inelastic); at P = 25, Q = 50, PED = −1 (unit elastic, midpoint); at P = 40, Q = 20, PED = −4 (elastic).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "total revenue (TR)"?
options: The factors influencing price elasticity of demand: number and closeness of substitutes, necessity or luxury, proportion of income spent on the good, time period and addictiveness/habit
The total amount received by firms from selling their output, equal to price × quantity sold
The distribution of the burden of an indirect tax between consumers and producers, which depends on PED and PES
Demand for which PED is greater than 1 (in absolute value), so quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than price
items.answer: The total amount received by firms from selling their output, equal to price × quantity sold
items.markingKey: B. "total revenue (TR)" is the total amount received by firms from selling their output, equal to price × quantity sold.

items.stem: Explain why primary commodity producers' revenues are very volatile.
items.answer: Demand and supply for commodities are both price inelastic, so supply shocks such as weather cause large price swings; with inelastic demand, a bumper harvest lowers price by more than quantity rises, reducing farmers' revenue.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Demand and supply for commodities are both price inelastic, so supply shocks such as weather cause large price swings; with inelastic demand, a bumper harvest lowers price by more than quantity rises, reducing farmers' revenue. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why primary commodity producers' revenues are very volatile.
items.answer: Demand and supply for commodities are both price inelastic, so supply shocks such as weather cause large price swings; with inelastic demand, a bumper harvest lowers price by more than quantity rises, reducing farmers' revenue. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Demand and supply for commodities are both price inelastic, so supply shocks such as weather cause large price swings; with inelastic demand, a bumper harvest lowers price by more than quantity rises, reducing farmers' revenue. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Demand for a city's public swimming pool is estimated to have PED = −1.6. The council wants more revenue. Advise whether it should raise or lower entry prices.
items.answer: Lower prices: demand is elastic, so a price cut raises quantity proportionately more, increasing total revenue.
items.markingKey: Lower prices: demand is elastic, so a price cut raises quantity proportionately more, increasing total revenue.

items.stem: With reference to the collapse in world cocoa prices in the late 1980s, explain how it illustrates PED and the revenue of primary commodity producers.
items.answer: Prices fell sharply after supply expanded; farmers in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana saw large falls in income. Inelastic demand meant greater output reduced prices more than proportionately, cutting producers' revenues.
items.markingKey: Context (Prices fell sharply after supply expanded; farmers in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana saw large falls in income.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Inelastic demand meant greater output reduced prices more than proportionately, cutting producers' revenues. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to PED and the revenue of primary commodity producers.

items.stem: Explain, with the help of a fully labelled diagram, why price inelastic demand and supply cause volatile prices and revenues for primary commodity producers.
items.answer: Diagram: steep (inelastic) demand and supply for coffee; a supply shift from good harvests (S1 to S2) causes a large fall in price and a small rise in quantity, so total revenue falls; a poor harvest does the reverse. Small shifts cause large price changes.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: steep (inelastic) demand and supply for coffee; a supply shift from good harvests (S1 to S2) causes a large fall in price and a small rise in quantity, so total revenue falls; a poor harvest does the reverse. Small shifts cause large price changes. IB Paper 1(a) markbands [10]: Level 4 (9-10) terms defined; clear, focused explanation; relevant, accurate and fully labelled diagram(s) that are explained. Level 3 (6-8) mostly accurate with some development. Level 2 (3-5) limited explanation or diagram errors. Level 1 (1-2) little understanding.

items.stem: Using diagrams, explain how the incidence of an indirect tax differs when demand is price elastic and when it is price inelastic, and explain the implications for government tax revenue.
items.answer: Inelastic demand: price rises by most of the tax, consumers bear most of the burden, quantity falls little – large revenue. Elastic demand: price rises little, producers bear most, quantity falls a lot – smaller revenue. Diagrams with S and S + tax, consumer and producer burden areas.
items.markingKey: Inelastic demand: price rises by most of the tax, consumers bear most of the burden, quantity falls little – large revenue. Elastic demand: price rises little, producers bear most, quantity falls a lot – smaller revenue. Diagrams with S and S + tax, consumer and producer burden areas.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

In 2023 Ghana's cocoa farmers sold 750,000 tonnes at an average of $2,500 per tonne. In 2024, poor weather cut output to 530,000 tonnes, but the world price rose to around $7,000 per tonne.
— Stylised figures based on 2023-2024 market conditions

Using the data, calculate the change in total revenue and explain what it implies about the PED for cocoa.
items.answer: TR rose from $1.875bn to $3.71bn. Price rose by 180% while quantity fell by about 29%: demand is price inelastic, so the supply shortage increased revenue (for producers able to sell at world prices).
items.markingKey: TR rose from $1.875bn to $3.71bn. Price rose by 180% while quantity fell by about 29%: demand is price inelastic, so the supply shortage increased revenue (for producers able to sell at world prices). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Explain why an indirect tax on a good with inelastic demand is ineffective in reducing consumption.
items.answer: Consumers are unresponsive to price, so although the price rises, quantity demanded falls only slightly; the tax mainly raises revenue rather than changing behaviour, at least in the short run.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Consumers are unresponsive to price, so although the price rises, quantity demanded falls only slightly; the tax mainly raises revenue rather than changing behaviour, at least in the short run. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Elena writes: "A firm should always raise its price to increase revenue." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A price rise raises revenue only if demand is price inelastic; with elastic demand, revenue falls.
items.markingKey: A price rise raises revenue only if demand is price inelastic; with elastic demand, revenue falls. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the government of Colombia might be concerned when world coffee prices fall by 30% in a year.
items.answer: Coffee demand and supply are price inelastic; farmers' revenues and export earnings fall sharply, reducing incomes in coffee-growing regions and tax revenue.
items.markingKey: Coffee demand and supply are price inelastic; farmers' revenues and export earnings fall sharply, reducing incomes in coffee-growing regions and tax revenue.

items.stem: Briefly describe Mexico's 2014 tax on sugary drinks and explain what it reveals about the effect of an indirect tax when demand is price inelastic.
items.answer: A tax of 1 peso per litre (about 10%) reduced purchases of taxed drinks by roughly 6-12% in the first years. Quantity fell by a smaller percentage than the price rose, so the tax raised substantial revenue while having a moderate effect on consumption.
items.markingKey: Context (A tax of 1 peso per litre (about 10%) reduced purchases of taxed drinks by roughly 6-12% in the first years.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Quantity fell by a smaller percentage than the price rose, so the tax raised substantial revenue while having a moderate effect on consumption. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the effect of an indirect tax when demand is price inelastic.

items.stem: A good with a YED of −0.6 is what?
items.answer: An inferior good
items.markingKey: An inferior good. Negative YED means demand falls as income rises.

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "A good with a YED of 0.4 is an inferior good because the value is less than one." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Any positive YED indicates a normal good; 0.4 means it is a necessity (income inelastic). Inferior goods have negative YED.
items.markingKey: Any positive YED indicates a normal good; 0.4 means it is a necessity (income inelastic). Inferior goods have negative YED. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how YED helps to explain the decline of the share of agriculture in employment as countries develop.
items.answer: Food has low YED; as incomes rise, spending shifts to manufactures and services with higher YED, so resources (labour) move out of agriculture into other sectors – sectoral change.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Food has low YED; as incomes rise, spending shifts to manufactures and services with higher YED, so resources (labour) move out of agriculture into other sectors – sectoral change. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A supermarket chain expects a recession. Using YED, explain which products it should stock more of.
items.answer: Products with negative YED (inferior goods, e.g. own-brand basics) will see demand rise; luxuries with high YED will see demand fall most.
items.markingKey: Products with negative YED (inferior goods, e.g. own-brand basics) will see demand rise; luxuries with high YED will see demand fall most.

items.stem: Leila writes: "A rise in income causes a movement along the demand curve." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Income is a non-price determinant; a change in income shifts the demand curve. YED measures the size of that shift.
items.markingKey: Income is a non-price determinant; a change in income shifts the demand curve. YED measures the size of that shift. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain, using the concept of YED, how a firm selling both luxury and budget product lines might be affected by a recession.
items.answer: Luxury lines (YED > 1) see demand fall by more than income; budget lines (YED < 0 or low) may see stable or rising demand; overall revenue less volatile; firms may shift marketing and production towards budget lines in recessions.
items.markingKey: Luxury lines (YED > 1) see demand fall by more than income; budget lines (YED < 0 or low) may see stable or rising demand; overall revenue less volatile; firms may shift marketing and production towards budget lines in recessions.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "Engel's law".
items.answer: The observation that as household income rises, the proportion spent on food falls, because food has income inelastic demand
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the observation that as household income rises, the proportion spent on food falls, because food has income inelastic demand. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a luxury and a necessity.
items.answer: Both are normal goods. For a necessity 0 < YED < 1 (demand rises less than proportionately with income); for a luxury YED > 1 (demand rises more than proportionately).
items.markingKey: Both are normal goods. For a necessity 0 < YED < 1 (demand rises less than proportionately with income); for a luxury YED > 1 (demand rises more than proportionately). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe the growth of China's middle class since 2000 and explain what it reveals about income elasticity of demand.
items.answer: Rapid income growth led to soaring demand for cars, overseas travel and dairy products, while demand for some staple grains per person stagnated. Goods with high YED (cars, tourism) grew much faster than income, while staples with low or negative YED did not.
items.markingKey: Context (Rapid income growth led to soaring demand for cars, overseas travel and dairy products, while demand for some staple grains per person stagnated.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Goods with high YED (cars, tourism) grew much faster than income, while staples with low or negative YED did not. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to income elasticity of demand.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that countries that rely on exporting primary commodities will inevitably fall behind those that export manufactured goods.
items.answer: Dependence on low-YED commodities is a disadvantage, but outcomes depend on which commodities and on how revenues are managed and used for diversification.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: low YED for food means slow growth in demand; volatile prices and revenues (low PED and PES); declining terms of trade (Prebisch-Singer). Arguments against: some commodities have high demand growth (lithium, copper for the energy transition); revenues can be invested in diversification (Botswana's diamonds, Chile's copper); commodity booms (2000s) raised incomes. Judgement: Dependence on low-YED commodities is a disadvantage, but outcomes depend on which commodities and on how revenues are managed and used for diversification. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "price elasticity of demand (PED)"?
options: A measure of the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the good's own price, calculated as %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP
A normal good with YED greater than 1, so demand rises by a larger percentage than income
How easily consumers can switch to an alternative product; the closer the substitutes, the more price elastic demand
Raw materials produced by agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining, such as wheat, coffee, copper and oil
items.answer: A measure of the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the good's own price, calculated as %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP
items.markingKey: A. "price elasticity of demand (PED)" is a measure of the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the good's own price, calculated as %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "total revenue (TR)".
items.answer: The total amount received by firms from selling their output, equal to price × quantity sold
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the total amount received by firms from selling their output, equal to price × quantity sold. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: What goods is likely to have the most price elastic demand?
items.answer: One particular brand of bottled water
items.markingKey: One particular brand of bottled water. A single brand has many close substitutes.

items.stem: A student claims that a good with a YED of 0.4 is an inferior good because the value is less than one. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Any positive YED indicates a normal good; 0.4 means it is a necessity (income inelastic). Inferior goods have negative YED.
items.markingKey: Any positive YED indicates a normal good; 0.4 means it is a necessity (income inelastic). Inferior goods have negative YED. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between price inelastic demand and price elastic demand.
items.answer: With elastic demand (|PED| > 1) the percentage change in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage change in price; with inelastic demand (0 < |PED| < 1) it is smaller.
items.markingKey: With elastic demand (|PED| > 1) the percentage change in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage change in price; with inelastic demand (0 < |PED| < 1) it is smaller. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the incidence on producers and the incidence of a tax on consumers.
items.answer: The consumer burden is the rise in price paid; the producer burden is the fall in price received after tax. The more inelastic side of the market bears more of the tax.
items.markingKey: The consumer burden is the rise in price paid; the producer burden is the fall in price received after tax. The more inelastic side of the market bears more of the tax. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between price elasticity of demand and slope of a demand curve.
items.answer: Slope measures the absolute change in price for a change in quantity and is constant on a straight line; PED measures proportional responsiveness and changes along the line.
items.markingKey: Slope measures the absolute change in price for a change in quantity and is constant on a straight line; PED measures proportional responsiveness and changes along the line. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why primary commodity producers may face falling relative incomes as the world economy grows.
items.answer: Demand for most primary commodities (especially food) is income inelastic, so as world incomes rise demand grows more slowly than for manufactures and services; commodity producers' share of world income falls.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Demand for most primary commodities (especially food) is income inelastic, so as world incomes rise demand grows more slowly than for manufactures and services; commodity producers' share of world income falls. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between price elastic demand and price inelastic demand.
items.answer: With elastic demand (|PED| > 1) the percentage change in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage change in price; with inelastic demand (0 < |PED| < 1) it is smaller.
items.markingKey: With elastic demand (|PED| > 1) the percentage change in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage change in price; with inelastic demand (0 < |PED| < 1) it is smaller. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe the collapse in world cocoa prices in the late 1980s and explain what it reveals about PED and the revenue of primary commodity producers.
items.answer: Prices fell sharply after supply expanded; farmers in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana saw large falls in income. Inelastic demand meant greater output reduced prices more than proportionately, cutting producers' revenues.
items.markingKey: Context (Prices fell sharply after supply expanded; farmers in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana saw large falls in income.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Inelastic demand meant greater output reduced prices more than proportionately, cutting producers' revenues. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to PED and the revenue of primary commodity producers.

items.stem: Using the UK's tobacco tax policy as an example, explain determinants of PED.
items.answer: Large, repeated increases in tobacco duty have raised substantial revenue because demand for cigarettes is price inelastic (estimates around −0.4 to −0.6). Addiction and lack of substitutes keep demand inelastic, so quantity falls by less than price and tax revenue rises.
items.markingKey: Context (Large, repeated increases in tobacco duty have raised substantial revenue because demand for cigarettes is price inelastic (estimates around −0.4 to −0.6).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Addiction and lack of substitutes keep demand inelastic, so quantity falls by less than price and tax revenue rises. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to determinants of PED.

items.stem: Briefly describe sectoral change in South Korea and explain what it reveals about sectoral change linked to YED.
items.answer: Agriculture's share of employment fell from about 50% in 1970 to around 5% today, while services grew to about 70% of employment. As incomes rose, spending shifted to manufactures and services with higher YED, pulling labour out of agriculture.
items.markingKey: Context (Agriculture's share of employment fell from about 50% in 1970 to around 5% today, while services grew to about 70% of employment.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.answer: Two diagrams with the same price rise from P1 to P2. Elastic demand (relatively flat curve): quantity falls by a larger percentage, from Q1 to Q2, |PED| > 1. Inelastic demand (relatively steep curve): quantity falls by a smaller percentage, |PED| < 1. Label axes P and Q, and the changes in each.

items.stem: A student claims that a straight-line demand curve has the same PED at every point. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: PED varies along a linear demand curve because P/Q changes: it is elastic at high prices, unit elastic at the midpoint and inelastic at low prices.
items.markingKey: PED varies along a linear demand curve because P/Q changes: it is elastic at high prices, unit elastic at the midpoint and inelastic at low prices. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Knowledge of PED is essential for firms setting prices."
items.answer: PED is valuable for pricing decisions, but estimates are imprecise and must be combined with knowledge of costs and rivals' behaviour.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows how revenue will change when price changes; helps target price discrimination; informs promotions and discounts. Arguments against: PED estimates are uncertain and change over time; competitors' reactions change outcomes; firms also consider costs, brand image and long-term objectives. Supported judgement: PED is valuable for pricing decisions, but estimates are imprecise and must be combined with knowledge of costs and rivals' behaviour.

items.stem: "Knowledge of PED is more useful to governments than to firms." Discuss.
items.answer: PED is essential to both: governments use it for tax design and firms for pricing; neither can do without it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: guides choice of goods for indirect taxes and predicts revenue; helps assess the effect of taxes on consumption of demerit goods. items.stem: To what extent is it true that Brand loyalty is the most effective way for a firm to reduce the price elasticity of demand for its product?
items.answer: Brand loyalty can reduce PED significantly, but it is costly to build and may erode; product differentiation and innovation also matter.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: loyal customers do not switch to substitutes; allows higher prices without large falls in sales. items.stem: Define the term "unit elastic demand".
items.answer: Demand for which PED equals 1, so the percentage change in quantity demanded equals the percentage change in price
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: demand for which PED equals 1, so the percentage change in quantity demanded equals the percentage change in price. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "tax incidence".
items.answer: The distribution of the burden of an indirect tax between consumers and producers, which depends on PED and PES
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the distribution of the burden of an indirect tax between consumers and producers, which depends on PED and PES. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The share of a consumer's budget spent on a good; the larger the share, the more price elastic demand tends to be"?
options: sectoral change
total revenue (TR)
proportion of income spent
primary commodities
items.answer: proportion of income spent
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of proportion of income spent.

items.stem: Distinguish between a necessity and a luxury.
items.answer: Both are normal goods. For a necessity 0 < YED < 1 (demand rises less than proportionately with income); for a luxury YED > 1 (demand rises more than proportionately).
items.markingKey: Both are normal goods. For a necessity 0 < YED < 1 (demand rises less than proportionately with income); for a luxury YED > 1 (demand rises more than proportionately). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between perfectly elastic demand and perfectly inelastic demand.
items.answer: Perfectly elastic demand (PED = ∞) is horizontal: any price rise reduces quantity to zero; perfectly inelastic demand (PED = 0) is vertical: quantity does not change with price.
items.markingKey: Perfectly elastic demand (PED = ∞) is horizontal: any price rise reduces quantity to zero; perfectly inelastic demand (PED = 0) is vertical: quantity does not change with price. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the effect when demand is inelastic and the effect of a price rise on revenue when demand is elastic.
items.answer: With elastic demand a price rise reduces TR because quantity falls proportionately more; with inelastic demand TR rises because quantity falls proportionately less.
items.markingKey: With elastic demand a price rise reduces TR because quantity falls proportionately more; with inelastic demand TR rises because quantity falls proportionately less. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Omar writes: "Goods that are necessities always have perfectly inelastic demand." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Necessities usually have inelastic demand, but rarely perfectly inelastic; consumers still buy somewhat less, or switch brands, when prices rise.
items.markingKey: Necessities usually have inelastic demand, but rarely perfectly inelastic; consumers still buy somewhat less, or switch brands, when prices rise. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "A rise in income causes a movement along the demand curve." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Income is a non-price determinant; a change in income shifts the demand curve. YED measures the size of that shift.
items.markingKey: Income is a non-price determinant; a change in income shifts the demand curve. YED measures the size of that shift. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that a bumper harvest always makes farmers better off because they sell more. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: With price inelastic demand the price falls proportionately more than quantity rises, so total revenue falls.

items.answer: Three demand diagrams. Luxury (YED > 1): large rightward shift. Necessity (0 < YED < 1): small rightward shift. Inferior good (YED < 0): leftward shift. In each, the new equilibrium price and quantity are shown with the original supply curve.

items.stem: With reference to the response of petrol demand to the 2022 price spike in Europe, explain how it illustrates price inelastic demand.
items.answer: Petrol prices rose by over 30% in many EU countries, yet the volume of fuel sold fell only slightly in the short run. Few substitutes in the short run (people must still commute) mean |PED| was low, so quantity responded much less than price.
items.markingKey: Context (Petrol prices rose by over 30% in many EU countries, yet the volume of fuel sold fell only slightly in the short run.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: The PED for the service sold by a ferry company in Oslo is −0.25. It currently charges $8 and sells 10,000 units a week, and is considering a price rise of 20%. Calculate the change in total revenue and advise whether, to maximise revenue, it should raise or lower its price.
items.answer: TR changes from $80000 to $91200 (change of $11200); to raise revenue it should raise price
items.markingKey: New P = 9.6; %ΔQ = −0.25 × 20% = −5% so Q = 9500 [1]; TR 80000 → 91200 [2]; demand is inelastic, so raise price [1].

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline why price elasticity of demand varies along a straight-line demand curve.
items.answer: Diagram: linear demand from the P-intercept to the Q-intercept, midpoint marked. Above the midpoint |PED| > 1 (elastic), at the midpoint |PED| = 1, below it |PED| < 1 (inelastic). Because ΔQ/ΔP is constant but P/Q falls as price falls, elasticity declines down the curve; total revenue is maximised at the midpoint.

items.stem: Real incomes in Vietnam rose by 6% while demand for air travel rose by 15%. Calculate YED and classify air travel.
items.answer: YED = 15/6 = 2.5: a luxury (income elastic normal good).
